extracted.intended_audience: political scientists, policymakers, civic educators, informed citizens and students of public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts normative and practical criteria for how public opinion, representative procedure, intelligence work, and appeals to reason should be organized and evaluated in modern democratic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared ideas for federal matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Federalism swings either towards imperial centralization or towards parochial anarchy wherever the union is not based on correct and commonly accepted ideas of federal matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas do not arise spontaneously. They must be pieced together by generalization based on analysis, and the instruments for that analysis have to be invented and tested by research. Stability of the union depends on cultivating commonly accepted, analytically derived ideas of federal affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming subjectivism of individual experience
rubrics_metrics.description: No reform... is truly radical which does not consciously provide a way of overcoming the subjectivism of human opinion based on the limitation of individual experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral devices or property-system changes do not reach the root; effective reforms must create conscious methods (education, intelligence, procedure) to move opinions beyond the limits of individual experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligence bureau as instrument for decision-makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Primarily, the intelligence bureau is an instrument of the man of action, of the representative charged with decision, of the worker at his work, and if it does not help them, it will help nobody in the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The real use of intelligence systems is as an aid to representative government and administration in politics and industry — to help those doing public business, not to burden every private citizen with expert reports. Secondary uses: general information and a check on the daily press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outsiders should judge procedure, not substantive relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: The outsider can arrive at judgments about whether these conditions are sound only on the result after the event, and on the procedure before the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ordinary citizen can ask experts whether relevant facts were duly considered; he cannot in most cases decide what is relevant. He can judge whether interested groups were properly heard, whether ballots were honestly taken, and whether the result was honestly accepted. Focus public scrutiny on procedure and results rather than technical substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid appealing to the uninformed public on intricate matters
rubrics_metrics.description: For the practice of appealing to the public on all sorts of intricate matters means almost always a desire to escape criticism from those who know by enlisting a large majority which has had no chance to know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: substituting mass publicity, loudest voices, skilful publicity men, or editorial space for informed judgment. Appeals to public sentiment on complex issues invite manipulation and confusion rather than sound decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use neutral chairs and expert mediation in representative discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the representative inside carry on discussion in the presence of someone, chairman or mediator, who forces the discussion to deal with the analyses supplied by experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative bodies should include mediators who confront partisans with men who control the facts and have dialectical skill to distinguish real perception from stereotype. This Socratic-style, expert-mediated dialectic disintegrates partisanship and untangles slogans into analyzable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base disputes on empirical data and standard statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitute for the words 'well paid' and 'exploited' a table showing what the different classes are paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When partisans make sweeping claims, require concrete evidence (wage tables, budgets, price statistics). Use official figures as a default within a forum, and direct technical exceptions to standing intelligence committees rather than letting rhetoric dominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public reporting when private data cannot be produced
rubrics_metrics.description: What is private does not interest us... and, therefore, issues a statement to the public announcing that the wages of workers in groups C and M are so-and-so much below the official minimum living wage, and that Judge Gary declines to increase them for reasons that he refuses to state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If private actors will not produce books or evidence, the public procedures should record the fact and the refusal, and report the official findings and the nature of objections. Lack of transparency must itself be part of the public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in naming and defining terms to objectify ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of naming, the effect, that is, of saying that the labor groups C and M, but not X, are underpaid, instead of saying that Labor is Exploited, is incisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define groups and terms precisely to disentangle emotion from fact. Naming converts 'my' prejudice into an object ('that') and makes ideas open to correction by new data. Encourage definition, specification, and the narrowing of vague, emotionally charged labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic gathering of social knowledge integrated with action
rubrics_metrics.description: The gathering of social knowledge is, on the whole, still haphazard; not, as it will have to become, the normal accompaniment of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence work should be organized because modern decision requires it; accumulation of systematic data will allow political science to generalize and provide teachers with working models. Make data-collection routine and tied to administrative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic education in critical reading and introspection
rubrics_metrics.description: He can teach the pupil to look in his newspaper for the place where the dispatch was filed, for the name of the correspondent, the name of the press service, the authority given for the statement... He can teach him the character of censorship, of the idea of privacy, and furnish him with knowledge of past propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach methods: check dispatch origin, correspondent identity, sourcing, circumstances of statements; ask whether reporter witnessed events; study censorship and past propaganda; use comparative history and anthropology to expose codes and stereotypes; use case method to foster habits of examining sources and introspection about imagery and allegory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reason central where time and stability permit; respect time-differential
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an element of time in politics... the relevancy of any plan depends upon the length of time the operation requires. The rate at which reason, as we possess it, can advance itself is slower than the rate at which action has to be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that reason and social science advance slowly compared to urgent political action; use reason in contexts with long-term stability and avoid expecting immediate rational deliberation in crises. Account for rate-of-change when proposing plans and distinguish false crises from real ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying
rubrics_metrics.description: Hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying are the seven deadly sins against public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In appeals to reason and in public discourse insist on decency and openness; these vices poison the appeal to reason and should be guarded against as long-run political liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate charity and decency as political dispositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where so much is uncertain, where so many actions have to be carried out on guesses, the demand upon the reserves of mere decency is enormous, and it is necessary to live as if good will would work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given unavoidable uncertainty, maintain charitable assumptions about others and a hearty prejudice against destructive attitudes; sustain belief in the possibility of improving human conduct and avoid despair that undermines long-term rational projects.
